notes: Volume P–R of the collection: 60 pages, 42 entries (21 under P, 21 under R) covering architects, builders, developers, a landscape architect, a preservationist, a curator and four firms, read end to end — the title page, the two letter indexes, every entry (education, firms, cultural identification, narrative and footnotes), every 'Projects in San Francisco' and 'Other notable projects' list, and every figure caption. The sixth of the eight letter-range PDFs; A–C, D–F, G–I, J–L and M–O are done. No inventory table and no APN anywhere. Seven entries yielded no numbered San Francisco address: Martha Jane Moorehead Parug, Hilde Reiss and Lutah Maria Riggs have no San Francisco work at all; Morton Rader's only San Francisco entry is the Chinatown Gate committee; Gee Gee Platt and Robert Royston are recorded for advocacy and for a Diamond Heights landscape given without a number; and Louis Polk's single project, the Jessie Street Substation rebuild, is given without a number. John Lyon Reid's four San Francisco projects are all given by campus or boulevard rather than by number. Powers and Ahnden has a full entry the P index does not list, and Arthur Francis Rousseau heads the R index with no entry anywhere in the volume — the same trap volume J–L hit with Alfred Henry Jacobs.

coverage.remaining: Volumes S–U and V–Z of the same collection — two more PDFs from the same landing page, each its own batch. Volumes A–C, D–F, G–I, J–L, M–O and P–R are finished.
coverage.note: 358 numbered-address mentions across 60 pages became 223 findings. The gap is the unnumbered and the repeated: John Lyon Reid's schools and hospital buildings, Timothy Pflueger's Transbay Terminal and Golden Gate International Exposition work, Percy & Hamilton's Sharon Building and several Rousseau tracts are given by campus, park or cross street with no street number, and Oliver Rousseau's list repeats the Marian Realty firm list almost entirely. 187 of the 223 reached a parcel and 36 did not: 16 numbers the city no longer has, 11 recorded ranges now split across separate parcels, 6 condominiums, 1 street the registry does not hold, 1 range printed in a form with no readable pair of numbers, and 1 given on Montgomery Avenue, which became Columbus Avenue in 1909. Of the 187, 126 were published onto 125 pages (49 created by this run) across 24 neighborhood directories, and 61 were declined: 56 already carried by a survey or statement that documented the building first, 4 undated pieces of work with no component to carry them, and 1 whose recorded number is not a readable pair and whose parcel already credits another architect. 54 pages state a construction-date disagreement with the assessor and 11 state, unadjudicated, a disagreement in the record itself or that the building described may not be the one standing.
